rationale: flops-1 is a tiny (542-byte text, 2 functions), extremely hot floating-point kernel from the SingleSource suite, so the dominant constraint is runtime overhead on a tight FP arithmetic loop, not per-function coverage. SUB gets the highest SecurityGain because arithmetic substitution directly obscures the FP computation that is the reverse engineer's primary anchor, while its low RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights keep it attractive even for the hot loop (its CorrectnessRisk is moderate since substitutions must not perturb FP rounding/strictness). SPLIT and IGV are nearly free transformations that add structural diversity and hide global references, so they are favored; IGV is kept slightly below SPLIT because this program has few globals. BCF, FLA, and IBR carry genuinely high per-execution costs (bogus branches, dispatch loops, indirect branching) that would be paid on every iteration of the flops loop for minimal additional confusion in straight-line numeric code, so their SecurityGain is deliberately suppressed and their RuntimeCost weights elevated so the selector applies them only if a function's features justify it; FLA is weakest because the target has almost no control-flow complexity to flatten. ICALL is largely disabled in effect: this binary has essentially no indirect-call surface (two tiny functions) so indirection buys little diversity while adding call overhead.
